text.p: Cigarette companies, bombarded by lawsuits and facing increasing restrictions on advertising, are finding new ways to promote their brands, industry experts said on Friday.
Tobacco product manufacturers are now branching out into everything from the clothing business to organising holidays.
Customers around the world can now garb themselves in Camel footwear and Marlboro branded clothing, buy music at Salem record stores, and book holidays through a Peter Stuyvesant travel agency.

They can watch sporting events ranging from car racing to snooker sponsored by major tobacco companies and redeem coupons from cigarette packs for various branded goods. In some markets consumers can still even see advertisements for cigarettes.
"We're reacting in whatever creative ways are open to us," Clive Turner, executive director of industry affairs for Britain's Tobacco Manufacturers' Association (TMA), told Reuters.
On Thursday, Liggett Group agreed to settle tobacco litigation in the United States with 22 of the 50 states in a move being seen as the harshest blow yet to the cigarette industry.
As Western countries have imposed more and more restrictions on cigarette companies, manufacturers have also increasingly turned to emerging markets in Eastern Europe and Asia.
But many of those markets are now mimicking the West and also clamping down on cigarette advertising.
China, which accounts for one-third of worldwide cigarette consumption, in 1995 imposed a total ban on cigarette advertising, including a ban on sponsorship.
Vietnam earlier this year reissued directives for a total ban on cigarette advertising and Bulgaria has plans to ban tobacco advertising on television.
France imposed Western Europe's toughest legislation in 1993 when it banned all direct and indirect advertising and promotion of cigarettes.
Radio and television advertising for tobacco products is banned in Germany and Britain, but outdoor advertising is still permitted -- and thriving.
Britain, however, severely limits the content of cigarette advertising, resulting in adverts that range from the highly creative to the highly mysterious.
"Some ads are so esoteric that unless you're a smoker you can't understand them -- and even if you're a smoker they're difficult to understand," said the TMA's Turner.
One advert shows a red motorcyle in the middle of a desert -- with nary a cigarette package in sight. "The motorcyle is red and that means it's Marlboro," said Turner.

The Marlboro brand, owned by Philip Morris Cos Inc, accounts for eight percent of worldwide cigarette consumption, said Chris Hancox, analyst for an upcoming World Tobacco report from Euromonitor, a market research group.

The global cigarette market grew more than 20 percent from 1992 to 1996 to reach $300 billion. Although the Chinese market grew 40 percent in that period, its growth has been slowing dramatically, dropping from 22 percent in 1994 to about three percent currently.
The advertising ban in China is curbing growth, but Hancox said it is not the major factor.

"Most of the evidence is the only thing that stops people smoking is higher and higher prices," said Hancox. A packet of cigarettes in China can be bought for as little as 10 cents, and as much as $2.00 for international brands.
The tobacco companies insist their adverts are aimed at winning market share from existing smokers rather than encouraging people to smoke. But even seemingly small market shifts are highly valuable.
"If you get a one percent change in market share (in Britain) that's about 100 million pounds in revenues," said TMA's Turner.
"We believe in advertising in that it allows us to compete for market share and communicate with our customers," said Jeff Jeffery, a spokesman for Gallaher Ltd American Brands Inc
